en: The Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of King Mañjarī, spoken by the Buddha.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang, by imperial decree.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavat was staying in Śrāvastī at the Jetavana Grove.
At the Anāthapiṇḍika Garden.
At that time, having arisen from meditative concentration, the World-Honored One expounded the unsurpassed, ambrosial, and wondrous Dharma for the fourfold assembly.
Then, an immeasurable multitude of hundreds of thousands surrounded him front and back; with their faculties unmoving, they listened to the essential points of the Dharma.
At that time, having seen that the great assembly was tranquil in body and mind and listening to the Dharma with earnest devotion, all the bhikṣus had doubts and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”
I only pray that, out of compassion, you will sever this web of doubt.

O Great Teacher, Unsurpassed Dharma King: for what reason do all those present here in this assembly listen to the sublime Dharma with such earnest devotion, their bodies and minds unmoving, as if drinking ambrosia?
The World-Honored One said:
"O bhikṣus! In the past, for the sake of seeking the Dharma, I was profoundly reverent in my heart."
Listen attentively! Reflect upon this well!
I shall explain the causes and conditions for you.

"In the distant past, in the great city of Vārāṇasī, there was a king named Suvarṇavarṇa who ruled the world according to the Dharma. The land was prosperous and joyful, and the population was flourishing;
it was free from warfare, deceit, and hostile thieves, and likewise devoid of the sufferings of illness or calamitous misfortunes.
Rice, sugarcane, cattle, and sheep abounded everywhere, and there were no shards, rubble, weeds, or thorns. He nurtured his millions of subjects with kindness as if looking upon an only son."

That king was respectful and faithful, with a noble and virtuous disposition; he benefited both himself and others, making firm vows, possessing a compassionate heart, longing for the Great Dharma, taking pity on the masses, and loving his officials. He eliminated stinginess and greed, always practicing great renunciation.
The king’s queen was named Miaorong (Wonderful Beauty); she was of upright countenance, her deportment was composed and deliberate, and she was perfected in all virtues, beloved by all.

The king had an only son named Duanzhengzi (Upright Son); though still young in years, he was loyal, filial, benevolent, and compassionate, and was so cherished by the king that he never left his side.
"Later, at another time, King Varṇa, his heart longing for the sublime Dharma, summoned his ministers and addressed them, saying:
'I have conceived a thirsting aspiration for the wondrous Dharma; you should seek it out for me.'"
Then the ministers came forward and addressed the king, saying: "Great King!
You should know that it is only when the Great Awakened World-Honored One appears in the world that there is the Sublime Dharma."
The king replied to his ministers, "Although there is no Buddha at present, try to seek one out for me.

Thereupon, the king immediately placed exquisite gold and jewels inside a casket and suspended it atop a banner; he then beat drums and issued a proclamation to announce far and wide to the four quarters:
"If there be anyone who shall proclaim the sublime Dharma for me, I shall reward their kindness with a golden casket and celebrate them with the performance of extensive music.
Thus he issued the summons, and much time passed, yet not a single person was able to preach the Dharma; the king remained there, dwelling in thirsting longing and sorrow.
"At that time, Śakra surveyed the lower realms to see who was virtuous and who was wicked,
and who remained untiring in their pursuit of the supreme cause.
He then beheld this king, distressed for the sake of the Dharma, and thought to himself:"
"This King of Wondrous Form has long yearned for the supreme Dharma; I shall test him to see whether his purpose is true or false.

He then transformed himself into a great yakṣa with hands, feet, and body unlike any other, and a face so terrifying that it struck fear into all. Coming into the midst of the assembly, he said to the king:
"You, O Benevolent One, seek the supreme Dharma; I am able to expound it."
Upon hearing the sound of the Dharma, the king was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; he addressed the yakṣa, saying: “Lord Guhyapati!
Since there is this sublime Dharma, I pray that you will explain it for me, and I shall listen attentively!”
The yakṣa replied:
"Great King, you have now conceived a slight attitude toward the Dharma, thinking that because it is easily obtained, you may command its proclamation.
Such is not the way things ought to be; my body is famished and empty—how could I possibly preach for you?"
Upon hearing these words, the king immediately commanded his chief cook to quickly serve up all the finest dishes.
The yakṣa declared, "The food from the royal kitchen is not what I eat; only the warm blood and flesh of humans are my regular fare."
The King said,
"How can human flesh and blood be obtained so suddenly? The yakṣa said:
"The king's beloved son should indeed be given to him.
Upon hearing these words, the king thought to himself:
"I have long sought the supreme Dharma with great hardship; now that I have heard the sound of the Dharma, it has become priceless."
At that time, the son Sundara was standing by his father’s side; having heard these words, he knelt and addressed the king, saying:
"I only pray, Father King, that you do not give way to grief or distress!"
"Whatever my father hopes for, I shall cause it to be fulfilled.
You may take my body to offer to Guhyapati, so that he may have it as food.
The king said:
"I see that you seek the Dharma and have renounced your beloved body.
Excellent, O noble man! Do as you please."
The handsome son immediately offered his own body to the yakṣa.
Having accepted it, the yakṣa, in the presence of the king and the great assembly, tore his body apart and devoured the flesh and drank the blood.
Although the king saw this, his devotion to the Dharma was so profound that he felt no fear or alarm at all.
Then Guhyapati spoke again to the king, saying:
"I am still not satiated; give me your wife as well."
At that time, Lady Miaorong was also by the king’s side; having heard these words, she likewise offered her own body to the yakṣa.
Once the yakṣa had accepted it, he devoured her flesh and blood, and then addressed the king, saying:
"I am still hungry and have not yet been satisfied."
The king then addressed him, saying: "Lord Guhyapati!
Having already given away my only son, and even after my wife has eaten again, she still says she is hungry and empty."
"Take whatever you wish; I am willing to provide it with a mind free from regret.
The yakṣa replied, "The King’s own body should be given as food to me."
The King said, “Excellent!
Truly I do not dare be stingy; however, once my body has perished, how shall I hear the Dharma?”
"Now, I shall first listen to his sublime Dharma; once I have received and upheld it, I shall immediately cast off this body.
At that time, the yakṣa made a pact with the king and, in the midst of a great assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis, spoke these excellent and wondrous verses:
"From craving arises sorrow; From craving arises fear."
"If one is free from craving, there is neither sorrow nor fear.
Having heard this sublime and wondrous Dharma, the king felt great joy and immeasurable gladness; he then addressed Guhyapati, saying:
"I have heard the Dharma and shall uphold it according to its teaching."
"Now, let this body of mine be eaten at your pleasure.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, seeing that the King’s body and mind were as immovable as Mount Sumeru for the sake of the Dharma, knew that he would surely realize unsurpassed awakening. Abandoning his yakṣa form and restoring his celestial appearance, his heart filled with faith and joy, he approached with a serene countenance; taking his son with one hand and his wife with the other, he addressed the King, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!

This virtuous man has donned firm armor to shatter the army of afflictions and deliver the ignorant and deluded from the sea of birth and death; observing such valor, he will surely before long be able to achieve unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"I now entrust your wife and children to you.
At that time, the king immediately said to Śakra, Lord of the Devas:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"O Lord of Devas, Kauśika!
Bestowing great compassion, you have acted as a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) and have already fulfilled my heart’s desire for the Dharma.
At that moment, Śakra, Lord of Devas, suddenly vanished from the midst of the great assembly.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"What do you think? Do not harbor any doubt:
the King of Wondrous Appearance at that time was none other than myself."
The handsome son was Rāhula; the wife of exquisite beauty was Yaśodharā.
You should know that in the past, for the sake of seeking the Dharma, I did not begrudge giving up my beloved wife, son, and even my own body—how much less so other things!
For this reason, all those in the great assembly who hear the Dharma from me at present listen with single-minded devotion and without weariness;
furthermore, because I formerly sought the Dharma while forgetting my own fatigue, I now preach the Dharma for the sake of the multitude throughout the long night without ever becoming weary.
"O bhikṣus, you should train yourselves after me: with reverence and respect, diligently seek the sublime Dharma;
having heard the Dharma, practice according to its teaching, and do not be negligent."
At that time, when the bhikṣus and the assembly of humans and devas had heard what the Buddha had spoken, they rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Thus concludes the *Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of King Suvarṇavarṇa* as spoken by the Buddha.
